---
title: "Language tour"
---

Seven small programs, one pillar each. Every program on this page ships in the
repo under `examples/`, every excerpt is taken from the real file, and every
output block is what the program actually prints. Run any of them yourself:

```bash
jestyrc run examples/life.jtr
```

All seven are part of the 148-file corpus that both compilers — the ~52K-line
Rust reference and the 29,818-line self-hosted compiler — must lower to
byte-identical C (single-file/concat emission path).

## Life: arrays are stack values

`examples/life.jtr` is Conway's Game of Life on a fixed 8x8 torus. There is no
heap anywhere in it. `[64]i32` is a plain value: it lives on the stack, copies
on assignment, and indexing is bounds-checked. `read` parameters are borrows
you never annotate with lifetimes — the compiler checks the aliasing, the
source just says who gets to write.

```{.rust}
fn step(read b: [64]i32) -> [64]i32 {
    var next: [64]i32 = [0; 64]
    var y: i32 = 0
    for y < H {
        var x: i32 = 0
        for x < W {
            let n: i32 = neighbors(b, x, y)
            let alive: i32 = b[idx(x, y)]
            if alive == 1 {
                if n == 2 or n == 3 { next[idx(x, y)] = 1 }
            } else {
                if n == 3 { next[idx(x, y)] = 1 }
            }
            x = x + 1
        }
        y = y + 1
    }
    return next
}
```

`board = step(board)` in `main` is just a value assignment — no clone call, no
move ceremony. The glider walks:

::: {.program-output}
```
.#......          ........
..#.....          ..#.....
###.....   ...    ...#....
........          .###....
........          ........
(gen 0)           (gen 4, three frames elided)
```
:::

## Calc: recursive ADTs and errors that carry data

`examples/calc.jtr` evaluates `(7 - 3) * (10 / 2)`. `indirect` boxes the
recursive children; `match` is exhaustive; the error set `!{ DivByZero(i64) }`
is part of the signature and its payload remembers the numerator that was about
to be divided. Dereferencing the raw child pointers is only legal inside
`unsafe { … }` — that boundary is a compile error to cross, not a convention.

```{.rust}
fn eval(read e: Expr) -> i64 !{ DivByZero(i64) } {
    match e {
        num(v)    => { return ok(v) },
        add(l, r) => {
            let a: i64 = eval(unsafe { l.* })?
            let b: i64 = eval(unsafe { r.* })?
            return ok(a + b)
        },
        // sub, mul elided — same shape
        div(l, r) => {
            let a: i64 = eval(unsafe { l.* })?
            let b: i64 = eval(unsafe { r.* })?
            if b == 0 { return err(DivByZero(a)) }
            return ok(a / b)
        },
    }
}

let w: i64 = eval(bad) catch |e| match e { DivByZero(n) => 0 - n }
```

The second evaluation is `42 / 0`; the `catch |e| match` recovers the payload
at the call site and prints its negation:

::: {.program-output}
```
20
-42
```
:::

## Primes: proven allocation-free, with contracts

`examples/primes.jtr` is a Sieve of Eratosthenes. `@no_alloc` is not a comment:
the compiler proves — transitively, through every call — that nothing inside
the function allocates, and rejects the program otherwise. `requires` and
`ensures` are design-by-contract clauses lowered to checked asserts.

```{.rust}
@no_alloc fn count_primes_below(n: i32) -> i32
    requires n <= 100
    ensures result >= 0
{
    var composite: [100]i32 = [0; 100]
    var count: i32 = 0
    var i: i32 = 2
    for i < n {
        if composite[i as usize] == 0 {
            count = count + 1
            var m: i32 = i * i
            for m < n {
                composite[m as usize] = 1
                m = m + i
            }
        }
        i = i + 1
    }
    return count
}
```

::: {.program-output}
```
25
10
2
29
97
```
:::

## Pi: parallel, and the answer never wavers

`examples/pi.jtr` throws 8,000 Monte Carlo darts across four spawned workers.
`concurrent { spawn … }` is structured concurrency: every task joins at the
closing brace, so no thread outlives the scope that made it. Each worker owns a
fixed-seed Lehmer generator and folds its hits in with `atomic_add`, so
scheduling order cannot reach the result.

```{.rust}
fn worker(hits: *mut i64, seed: i64) {
    var s: i64 = seed
    var mine: i64 = 0
    var i: i64 = 0
    for i < SAMPLES_PER_WORKER {
        s = lehmer(s)
        let x: i64 = s % R
        s = lehmer(s)
        let y: i64 = s % R
        if x * x + y * y < R * R { mine = mine + 1 }
        i = i + 1
    }
    atomic_add(hits, mine)
}

concurrent {
    spawn worker(hits, 1)
    spawn worker(hits, 20260807)
    spawn worker(hits, 48271)
    spawn worker(hits, 777)
}
```

::: {.program-output}
```
6300
3150
```
:::

::: {.claim}
This parallel program printed the same two numbers in 20 consecutive runs on
one machine, and the project's cross-OS determinism canary — a digest over a
much larger program exercising the whole numeric stack, parallel reductions
included — is byte-identical on Windows/MinGW-gcc and
Ubuntu 24.04/gcc 13.3.0, pinned by CI on every push.
<span class="verify">$ jestyrc run examples/pi.jtr</span>
:::

## Histogram: strings without copies

`examples/histogram.jtr` counts word lengths in a sentence. `split` never
allocates: each `w` is a `str` — a zero-copy view into the original text.
Owned `String` and borrowed `str` are distinct types, so "who frees this" is
answered by the type, not by convention.

```{.rust}
let text: str = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog and naps in warm golden afternoon sun"

var counts: [12]i32 = [0; 12]
var words: i32 = 0
for w in split(text, " ") {          // each `w` is a zero-copy view into `text`
    let n: usize = w.len
    if n < 12 { counts[n] = counts[n] + 1 }
    words = words + 1
}
```

::: {.program-output}
```
16
2 | #
3 | ######
4 | ####
5 | ###
6 | #
9 | #
```
:::

## Ledger: traits whose contracts include failure

`examples/ledger.jtr` puts two account types behind one trait — and the error
set `!{ Insufficient(i64) }` is written into the trait method itself, so every
implementation must honor it and every caller must handle it. `spend[T:
Account]` is monomorphized per type: no vtable, no allocation, and the payload
reports how much was actually available when a withdrawal fails.

```{.rust}
trait Account {
    fn withdraw(read self, amt: i64) -> i64 !{ Insufficient(i64) }
}

impl Account for Savings {
    fn withdraw(read self, amt: i64) -> i64 !{ Insufficient(i64) } {
        let avail: i64 = self.balance - self.reserve
        if amt > avail { return err(Insufficient(avail)) }
        return ok(self.balance - amt)
    }
}

fn spend[T: Account](read acct: T, amt: i64) -> i64 {
    return acct.withdraw(amt) catch |e| match e {
        Insufficient(avail) => 0 - avail,
    }
}
```

Negative numbers below are refusals — the payload, negated, saying what the
account actually held:

::: {.program-output}
```
70
-20
85
-100
```
:::

## Arena points: regions free in O(1)

`examples/arena_points.jtr` does geometry scratch work in a bump arena.
`region r { … }` owns the arena; `region_alloc` hands back `&[r]Point` — a
plain pointer with zero per-deref cost, safe because the compiler confines it
to the region's scope. Try to return one and you get a compile error
(`examples/region_escape.jtr` demonstrates the rejection). At the closing
brace the whole arena frees at once: no per-node frees, no leaks possible.

```{.rust}
region r {
    var a: &[r]Point = region_alloc(r, Point, Point { x: 0, y: 0 })
    var b: &[r]Point = region_alloc(r, Point, Point { x: 3, y: 4 })
    var c: &[r]Point = region_alloc(r, Point, Point { x: 10, y: 1 })
    var d: &[r]Point = region_alloc(r, Point, Point { x: 7, y: 9 })

    var route: i64 = 0
    route = route + manhattan(a.*, b.*)     // 7
    route = route + manhattan(b.*, c.*)     // 10
    route = route + manhattan(c.*, d.*)     // 11
    print_int(route)                        // 28
}                                            // the whole arena is gone, in O(1)
```

::: {.program-output}
```
28
16
```
:::
